extracted.intended_audience: aspiring crime/noir/thriller writers and readers interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on constructing a 'perfect' hardboiled/noir thriller by combining stylistic, character, thematic, and point-of-view ingredients drawn from canonical crime novels. Focuses on prose style, character pairings, feminine power, psychological depth, and racial/social perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic detective partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a couple who are busy falling or being in love while simultaneously chasing the killers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled on Nick and Nora Charles from The Thin Man: a partnership both romantic and intelligent whose interaction animates the story. Their relationship should produce witty, sarcastic, revealing dialogue and create an energetic, invested center to the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue that sings as well as growls
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should be witty, sarcastic, elegant—more like an elegant form of dancing than mere conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue ought to reveal character and relationship while propelling tone; it must be entertaining and tough at once ("sings as well as growls"). Use sharp repartee and subtext to show affection and danger simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spare, biting, cynical prose style
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a clear, hard, precise, gritty, unadorned style—"more Hemingway than Hemingway"—that embodies the hardboiled voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate the classically economical hardboiled diction exemplified by Raymond Chandler's early chapters (e.g., The Big Sleep). The opening paragraphs should be a 'master class in hardboiled style'—clean, vivid, and authoritative—so the first chapter hooks the reader immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feminine power and intuition (dames as leads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature powerful, instinctive, intelligent women not limited to supporting roles—women can lead, outthink, and be central to resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspired by Dorothy B. Hughes' In a Lonely Place: show psychological insight via fine details (tone of voice, facial expression, body language). Present women as courageous, intellectually capable agents rather than stereotypes; consider female accomplices and nontraditional detective figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view experimentation (flipping hunter/hunted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider telling the story from an unexpected vantage, e.g., the perpetrator's perspective rather than the detective's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inverting the usual POV (as Hughes does by adopting the murderer Dix Steele's perspective) can produce chilling psychological immediacy and moral ambiguity. Use POV choice to deepen tension and unsettle reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological depth and inward mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the central mystery as much about inner lives, family trauma, guilt, and psychological motives as about external clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ross MacDonald (Black Money) shows that the 'true mystery lay within the characters.' Use family histories, buried emotions, and psychological backstory to drive motive and reveal crime as outcome of personal/familial forces rather than only external plot machinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic richness: wealth, poverty, fate, and choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Weave socio-economic and philosophical themes—wealth vs. poverty, fate vs. personal choice—into the narrative's moral texture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let these themes inform character decisions and the novel's moral landscape. Use them to complicate culpability, motivate characters, and add layers beneath the procedural surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race, social perspective, and diverse protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate racial and social justice dimensions and broaden who can be a detective—protagonists of color must be able to see things others cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in Walter Mosley's Devil in a Blue Dress, foreground how race shapes detection and danger ("a world made doubly treacherous"). Use a protagonist whose social position yields different perceptions and stakes; address structural and interpersonal racism as part of plot and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elemental cynicism and moral ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed the noir's signature cynicism and ambiguity so moral certainties are eroded and characters operate in grey zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardboiled noir often resists clear moral resolution; cultivate ambiguity in motives, outcomes, and justice. Let the world feel morally compromised and the narrator/worldview skeptical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seductive opening and haunting aftertaste
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with paragraphs that 'seduce' the reader and craft a narrative that 'holds them captive until the last word and then haunts them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize a first chapter that acts as a 'hook'—evocative, stylish, and character-revealing. Structure the novel to sustain tension and resonance so the ending lingers emotionally and thematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as locus of mystery (detective as revealing figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make detection as much an act of understanding character as solving puzzles; the detective's temperament, clarity, and code shape the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a detective voice (e.g., Phillip Marlowe) whose personal code, world-weariness, and precise outlook are embedded in prose style and narrative stance. Let characterization of the investigator drive tone and reader alignment.
